name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,267

clue.text: Resolute company

blocks.note: first meaning: steadfast, not yielding
second meaning: a business

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a determined business, but they are two separate meanings of one word, one an adjective and one a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means unwavering as an adjective and a commercial business as a noun, so it fits both halves.

clue.text: Blooming common thing to be doing on Shrove Tuesday?

definitions.text: common thing to be doing on Shrove Tuesday

blocks.note: first meaning: a mild British intensifier, as in 'blooming cheek'

blocks.clueFragment: common thing to be doing on Shrove Tuesday
blocks.note: second meaning: tossing pancakes, the custom of Pancake Day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' suggests flowers in spring; here it is the mild British expletive. Shrove Tuesday, the day before Lent, is Pancake Day in Britain, when pancakes are tossed in the pan.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a polite British swear-word intensifier and the action of tossing pancakes over in a pan.

clue.text: Fend off horrible person partly on the rise

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the letters sit inside consecutive words
in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom upward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone tries to drive away an unpleasant person who is gaining ground.
explanation.walkthrough: LEPER is hidden in 'horribLE PERson'; reading it upwards gives REPEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel an attacker is to drive them back or ward them away successfully.

clue.text: Cavers moved east around small crack in a glacier

indicators.note: things that are moved change place, so the letters are rearranged
going around something encloses it, so one part wraps another

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the compass abbreviation for east
S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: Potholers shift eastward around a small fissure in an ice sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVERS plus E are rearranged to CREVASE, and S goes inside to make CREVASSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A crevasse is the deep open fissure that forms in glacier ice as it moves and stretches.

clue.text: Spoke really aggressively at first on phone

indicators.note: what comes first is the opening letter, so each of these words gives its initial

blocks.note: the opening letters of the two words
to dial is to phone someone

explanation.surface: Someone talked very belligerently at the start of a telephone call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoke' reads as the past tense of speak, but it is a noun: the rod of a wheel. In a down clue 'on' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: A radial is a line running out from a centre, and a wheel spoke is exactly such a line.

clue.text: Given attire distributed for dressing

indicators.note: something distributed is spread out and dealt around, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Clothes are handed out for people to get dressed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attire' and 'dressing' pull towards clothes; the dressing is the one poured on a salad.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinaigrette is an oil and vinegar mixture used as a salad dressing.

clue.text: Illustration, for example?

blocks.note: surface reading: a picture offered as an instance of something
setter's reading: the word 'illustration' stands for the word 'example', since the two mean the same

explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like it asks for a kind of picture; instead it treats the two words as words, one of which can stand in for the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Words with the same meaning, like illustration and example, are each a word of equivalent sense for the other.

clue.text: Imitate head of entertainment on radio broadcast?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, its opening letter
radio operators replace each letter with a code word, so a letter is swapped for its spoken name

blocks.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A mimic copies the voice of a station's entertainment chief on air.
explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO phonetic alphabet used on radio, the letter E is spoken as Echo.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo someone is to repeat or copy what they say or do, a synonym for mimicking.

clue.text: Blocked current politician meeting senior journalist more than once

indicators.note: this phrase says the preceding element appears twice in succession

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
Member of Parliament
short for editor
the same piece again

explanation.surface: A politician is prevented from meeting a newspaper editor repeatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: I is the physics symbol for current; 'more than once' doubles the editor.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impeded has been hindered or obstructed, the same as blocked in its path.

clue.text: Place of control in advertising, possibly

indicators.note: 'possibly' offers one possible version of the letters, so they can be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders where the real power lies in the ad business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In advertising, possibly' reads like a qualifier on a job role; the single word holds exactly the eleven letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the driving seat is the idiom for being in charge, the position from which things are steered.

clue.text: Some tension in the last inning of baseball game

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, a run inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the middle word into the last

explanation.surface: Nerves fray at the climax of a ball game.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in 'tensioN IN THe'; 'the' does double duty in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A regulation baseball game has nine innings, so the ninth is the final one.

clue.text: Task of certain workers is to survey one group of people

blocks.note: an opinion poll is a survey
Roman numeral one
a people forming one country

explanation.surface: Some employees are assigned to canvass a group of people.
explanation.walkthrough: The workers are worker bees, not office staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Worker bees carry pollen from flower to flower, so fertilising plants is their job.

clue.text: Fruit in Massachusetts, North Dakota, Arkansas, and Indiana

blocks.note: postal code for Massachusetts
postal code for North Dakota
postal code for Arkansas
postal code for Indiana

explanation.surface: A fruit is grown across several American states.
explanation.walkthrough: Each state gives its two-letter US postal abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandarin is a small loose-skinned citrus fruit, close kin of the tangerine.

clue.text: Foolish individual turned in another foolish individual

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
a twit is a silly person

explanation.surface: One fool reports another fool to the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned in' looks like betrayed to the police; 'in' is the piece that is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitwit is a silly, stupid person, a synonym for a fool.

clue.text: Clothing items from this new designer didn’t impress, ultimately

indicators.note: a new version is a remade one, so the letters take a fresh order
what comes ultimately comes last, so each word gives its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A fresh designer's garments failed to win over the critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New designer' reads as a newcomer to fashion; 'new' applies only to the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: T-shirts are casual short-sleeved tops, everyday garments of the kind called clothing items.

clue.text: Piracy perhaps alongside a peninsula

indicators.note: placing one thing alongside another sets them side by side in sequence

blocks.note: piracy is one example of a crime
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pirates operate off the coast of a peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks piracy as one example of the wider category.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimea is the peninsula jutting into the Black Sea from southern Ukraine.

clue.text: Circles round harbour somewhere in Iberia

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so the outer pieces enclose the inner one

blocks.note: each circle is the round letter O
a port is a harbour

explanation.surface: Rings are drawn round a harbour on a map of Spain and Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: Oporto is the older English name for Porto in Portugal, which fittingly contains a port.
explanation.definitionFit: Oporto is a city in northern Portugal, and Portugal forms part of the Iberian peninsula.

clue.text: Shrill publicity stunt was irritating, we’re told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: hype is showy publicity, and something that itched was irritating

explanation.surface: A noisy marketing gimmick got on people's nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, HYPE ITCHED runs together into HIGH-PITCHED.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrill sound is piercingly high in tone, which is what a high-pitched noise is.

clue.text: Temporary setback had an effect on church

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: something that hit had an impact
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A brief reversal of fortune made a mark on the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had an effect' as in a policy that hit hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitch is a minor snag or delay that holds things up for a while.

clue.text: Cut legs when climbing

indicators.note: climbing goes upward, and in a down clue that reads the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: pins is informal British slang for legs

explanation.surface: A climber's legs get gashed on the way up.
explanation.walkthrough: Pins is a jokey British word for legs, as in 'wobbly on my pins'.
explanation.definitionFit: To snip is to cut with a quick small stroke of scissors.

clue.text: Caregiver periodically on our roster

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A carer shows up on the staff rota now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignoring the spaces, take every second letter starting with the second: oN oUr RoStEr.
explanation.definitionFit: A nurse is a trained professional who looks after the sick, a classic caregiver.

clue.text: Tenant takes time at the end to come back inside

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a tenant rents a home
the final letter

explanation.surface: A lodger finally gets round to returning home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time at the end' looks like 'eventually'; it is the last letter of 'time', slipped into RENTER after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-enter is to go into a place again after leaving, returning indoors.

clue.text: Job arrangement

blocks.note: first meaning: a post of employment
second meaning: the way things are placed or set out

explanation.walkthrough: Together the words sound like a work contract, but they are two separate meanings of one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means both a post someone holds at work and the placement or layout of things.

clue.text: Object almost entirely lacking in solidity

indicators.note: almost all of something stops just short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: an object is a thing

explanation.surface: Someone objects that an argument has almost no substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb meaning protest; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Something thin, like a watery soup or a weak excuse, lacks body or substance.
